 These Flyers may be worse than the worst team in franchise history
 There are a lot of glaring similarities between the 2026-27 Philadelphia Flyers through 19 games, and the 2006-07 Flyer team that ended up with just 56 points. We take a look at the two seasons, and if this season is heading in the same direction.
 Posted on November 9, 2026 November 9, 2026 by Jason MacNeil 
 Courtesy: Heather Barry Photography 
 As they enter Monday night’s game on the road against the lowly Vancouver Canucks, the 2026-27 version of the Philadelphia Flyers is looking like a shadow of the club that fought their way into the third seed of the Metropolitan Division. And won a playoff round to boot. The current team is beginning to mirror a club that nobody really wishes to think about ever again: the 2006-07 version of the Philadelphia Flyers. That version finished the 82-game season with a horrific 22-48-12, good enough for 56 points and fifth in the Atlantic Division (which Philadelphia was once a part of). 
 Perhaps there are a myriad of ways to compare this club with the one Ken Hitchcock coached for all of eight games before he was fired 20 years ago. John Stevens picked up the slack and went the rest of the way with the club featuring an aging (and injured) Peter Forsberg, two youngsters in Mike Richards and Jeff Carter, and Simon Gagne, who went on to score 41 goals for the Flyers that season. There is one subtle difference between the 2026-27 Flyers and the 2006-07 version. Through 19 games, the 2006-07 club had five wins to their credit (5-12-2). This current team? Well, what’s one less than five? And there are obvious rumblings about the need for head coach Rick Tocchet to be relieved of his duties before things spiral further out of control. The noise around Hitchcock was quickly silenced with his axing.
 Other similarities? Some are comical. Twenty years ago, Philadelphia started their season being shut out 4-0 by the Pittsburgh Penguins on the road. This year, it was 7-0 against Pittsburgh, before a hometown crowd that was eager to pick up where the playoff buzz left off. And prior to the 2006-07 season starting, Flyers general manager Bobby Clarke (who resigned when Hitchcock was fired) was busy with an offer sheet. Clarke attempted to lure Vancouver forward Ryan Kesler with a one-year $1.9 million deal. At the time, Kesler had just one year of play under his belt, but scored 10 goals to go with 13 assists in his rookie year. He looked like he could be a diamond in the rough. It was enough for Clarke to make the offer. Vancouver matched the deal. As we all know, this past summer current general manager Danny Briere attempted to lure Anaheim’s Leo Carlsson with a five-year, $90 million deal. It took a few days, but Philadelphia’s hopes were squashed when Anaheim matched the deal.
 The numbers
 Without going too far down the statistical rabbit hole, there are a number of numbers which make this current season on par (or possibly even worse) than how 2006-07 turned out. Granted, the fact Philadelphia has two more games to work with being an 84-game regular season could mean they end up with more points over the year. Or losses, and a worse points percentage. 
 Season Games Wins Losses OTL/SOL Points Goals For Goals Against 
 2006-07 19 5 12 2 12 46 74 
 2026-27 19 4 10 5 13 42 65 
 As you can see above, there’s not a lot to be hopeful about when it comes to crunching the basic numbers for both seasons. This year’s team has one more point, but one fewer win over 19 contests. They have also scored fewer goals, although they’ve allowed nine fewer over the same amount of time. In 19 games back in 2006-07, Philadelphia scored four or more goals on five occasions, including in two of their first three games. They were annihilated by Buffalo 9-1, and exacted revenge against Pittsburgh after the aforementioned 4-0 shutout loss by, er, getting trounced 8-2 at home. This year’s club, outside of the 7-0 loss, hasn’t been shelled. But they’ve only scored four or more goals on two occasions: a 6-3 win over Utah, and a 5-4 loss to Anaheim. 
 Season Goals For/Game Goals Against/Game Goal Differential/Game Shots For/Game Power Play Percentage Penalty Kill
Percentage 
 2006-07 2.42 3.89 -1.47 31.6 11.3 87.9 
 2026-27 2.21 3.42 -1.21 24.1 17.2 80.6 
 If it wasn’t news before, the Flyers aren’t scoring a whole lot of goals this year. Considering they are scoring less per game then they did 20 years ago should be very concerning. It was an issue last season, but Tocchet’s system and tight defensive structure — as well as the outstanding season Dan Vladar had — was enough to get Philadelphia to play near perfect 60-minute defensive gems more often than not. That the goals against is as bad as it is, but not as bad as 2006-07, should be of little consolation. It could be far worse if Vladar or Joseph Woll didn’t play as well as they did during the nine-game streak that set off this ongoing nightmare.
 As for the special teams, the Flyers are faring a bit better this year versus the 2006-07 Flyers with the man advantage. On the other hand, the penalty kill this season leaves a bit more to be desired versus what Philadelphia delivered in the opening 19 games two decades ago. On the whole, both clubs resembled teams that were at best slowly drowning. And at worst, heading for a major collapse.
 The players
 It’s foolish and impossible to compare players of different eras on different clubs, even if they wore the same jersey decades apart. In 2006-07, Philadelphia used 49 different players to get through the arduous season. So far through 19 games, the Flyers have used 30 different players. Injuries may see that number increase in the remaining 65 games. Or, if Briere decides to take a very hard second look at what he has on the team, and what direction he plans to go, more trades for more picks or prospects could result in a handful more newcomers, or callups from Lehigh Valley, to rival the turnover 20 years ago. 
 The 2006-07 club saw two youngsters in Jeff Carter and Mike Richards take their first baby steps to becoming fan favorites and darlings of the club. Through Carter’s first 19 games of that year, he had three goals and eight assists for 11 points. Meanwhile, Richards wasn’t feeling it at all in one category. The forward had eight assists also over his first 19 games, but had three in game 19 that year alone. Richards also had a horrible goal drought, scoring his first goal of the season on Nov. 24 of that year against Columbus, 23 games into the season. But both Richards and Carter would become cornerstones of the club, at least until they were both traded away on the same day a few years later. That summer they selected Claude Giroux twenty-second overall in the 2006 draft, even if Clarke couldn’t remember the forward’s name. It seemed dark at the time, but there was reason for hope with Giroux, Carter, and Richards.
 This 2026-27 Flyers roster features Matvei Michkov who is second in scoring with 10 goals and three assists for 13 points. So Michkov is further along in his point total than Carter and Richards in their respective season. But Porter Martone might be on pace with the duo, as through 19 games he has three goals and five assists for eight points. Elsewhere, Denver Barkey (who will play his seventeenth game Monday night against Vancouver barring something unexpected), has a pair of goals and six helpers for eight points. In short, there are some similarities with both seasons: a club that was struggling but were essentially tying their wagons to a few young talents for potential down the road.
 When the 2006-07 season ended, Philadelphia had two players with more than 20 goals: Gagne (41), and Mike Knuble (24). They also had six players who had 10 or more goals: Richards (10), Forsberg (11), Carter (14), Geoff Sanderson (11), R.J. Umberger (16), and Sami Kapanen (11). This year, outside of Michkov, every other Flyer skater will be hard pressed to hit 20 goals at their current pace. A more likely situation is between 10 to 15 goals, with Martone, Trevor Zegras, Christian Dvorak, Barkey, Tyson Foerster, and Owen Tippett hitting that range if this first quasi-quarter of the season is a measuring stick.
 The outcome?
 As 2006-07 progressed, and any chances of a playoff spot shot to hell, general manager Paul Holmgren set about cleaning the cupboards of veterans, and getting some prospects, picks, and youth in return. Forsberg was shipped off to Nashville for players and picks. Alexei Zhitnik went to Atlanta with Philadelphia getting Braydon Coburn in return. Martin Biron was picked up for a second-round pick. Simply put, Holmgren realized the club couldn’t continue in its current state, and changes needed to be made.
 How the rest of 2026-27 goes is unknown. It seems quite evident that if Briere defends Tocchet to the hilt to Flyers Governor Dan Hilferty and company, then he might be putting himself in danger of also being relieved of his duties. The more obvious option would be to thank Tocchet for his service, and finish the season at some point with an interim coach, or somebody who can try to spin this club in the right direction. Nobody is going to survive a season where a team is winning less than one-quarter of their games, even if they’re in the second year of a five-year deal. In addition to the coaching dilemma, Briere has to realize he can’t bring back the exact same club next year and expect a vastly different result. The Flyers are playing a very boring, bad brand of hockey. And outside of Michkov, Martone, Barkey, and Cole Knuble, a lot of nights the team would be unwatchable.
 The bigger question might be how Briere navigates the rest of this season. He’s put himself in a bind somewhat, with a lot of players who may not fit the bill in terms of the future locked into lengthy contracts. Then again, hindsight being what it is, he would’ve looked foolish to not lock up Trevor Zegras and Jamie Drysdale to contract extensions, not to mention Dan Vladar. Even with a huge increase in the cap ceiling, a lot of teams might bypass some players Briere could dangle in trade discussions in order to strip things down somewhat, and try to build with more high-end youth. That’s not to say the Flyers are over the hill, as they have one of the youngest teams in the league.
 Briere clearly intimidated the Flyers could take a step back this year, and was ridiculed for the remark as a result. And as is the case with many young teams, there’s no straight line to becoming a contender. Perhaps this season is an exception, and Philadelphia enters the 2027-28 season with a few more high-end pieces thanks to the draft. The Flyers are in the lottery discussion right now, and if the losses keep stacking up, those balls will only heighten their chances of the top pick. One only hopes that the ghosts of the 2007 draft don’t appear. That year, Philadelphia looked to be the odds-on favorites to land the top pick, and take Patrick Kane. However, Chicago won the draft, Philadelphia took James van Riemsdyk with the second pick overall, and Kane would show his talent against Philadelphia in 2010.
 If there is any silver lining one might take from these two seasons being compared, it’s this one nugget of information. After a 45-point decline from 2005-06 to 2006-07, the Flyers licked their wounds after a terrible season and rebounded in a big way. In 2007-08, Philadelphia finished with 95 points (a 39-point uptick), and lost in the Conference Finals. The demise of 2006-07 was short-lived, and a blip on the overall radar. Ideally, the Flyers begin to realize what is and is not working, and act accordingly. Briere has to realize this season, like it did back in 2006-07 is slowly slipping away. And he can’t act hastily, sacrificing the future to get Philadelphia off the basement floor this season. 
 There’s 65 games remaining this season, and if the first 19 are any indication, it’s going to be a very bumpy ride. Philadelphia entered the year hoping to make a statement. They’re doing just that: they’re not ready. Not by a longshot.
